title: Non-equilibrium dissipative stabilization of s- and d-wave superconductivity
authors: Aleksey Lunkin, Yury Holubeu, Denis Golež, Zala Lenarčič
abstract: Stabilizing superconductivity beyond its equilibrium regime has been one of the quests of nonequilibrium state engineering. We report the presence of nonthermal pairing gap in BCS superconductors coupled to two thermal baths, where one of the baths can be at a temperature well above the equilibrium $T_c$. Superconducting state is enabled by a highly non-equilibrium steady state stabilized by weak coupling to baths that break detailed balance condition. The steady-state is well described by a generalized Gibbs ensemble parametrized with chemical potentials for associated Bogoliubov quasiparticle. A strong, non-perturbative effect is reported for both $s$-wave and $d$-wave superconductors, and its possible realization in cavity-based experiments is discussed.
summary: This work explores stabilizing superconductivity in non-equilibrium steady states by coupling a BCS superconductor to two baths at potentially different temperatures. By solving the master equation using a Generalized Gibbs Ensemble, the authors show that the superconducting gap can remain finite even when one bath is super-critical. This highlights a powerful method for engineering quantum phases using controlled dissipation.
main_problem: The paper investigates how to stabilize superconducting states beyond their equilibrium critical temperatures by coupling the system to two distinct thermal baths.
main_result: A finite superconducting order parameter can be maintained even when one bath is at a temperature above the equilibrium critical temperature, demonstrating non-equilibrium stabilization.
method: The analysis employs the Generalized Gibbs Ensemble (GGE) approach, solving self-consistency equations derived from the Lindblad master equation governing quasiparticle occupation numbers.
model_or_system: The system is a BCS superconductor (s- and d-wave) coupled to two thermal baths ($T_1, T_2$). The dynamics are modeled using a Lindblad master equation and solved via time propagation or steady-state self-consistency.
key_observables: The superconducting order parameter (gap function, $\Delta$), and the steady-state quasiparticle occupation numbers ($n_{p,\sigma}$).
important_parameters: Bath temperatures ($T_1, T_2$), coupling strengths ($\gamma_0$), and the imbalance parameter $\alpha$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is the validity of the GGE Ansatz, which assumes quasiparticles are well-defined on intermediate timescales.
figures_summary:
Figures demonstrate the finite steady-state gap ($\Delta_\infty$) for s-wave superconductors when $T_1 
eq T_2$, and compare GGE predictions against thermal Gibbs Ensemble results.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from setting up the non-equilibrium master equation and GGE ansatz, deriving the steady-state self-consistency equations, and finally analyzing the results for both s-wave and d-wave symmetries across varying bath temperatures and coupling parameters.
why_interesting: The use of non-equilibrium steady states to engineer quantum phases is a key topic in open quantum systems, providing a concrete example of how thermal baths can be utilized beyond simple thermalization.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Steady-state gap ∆∞(in units of zero temperature gap ∆0) as a function of temperatures of the first bath T1 and second bath T2. For an s-wave superconductor, we find new non-equilibrium solutions at T1 ̸= T2 with finite gap despite one of the baths being at a temperature larger than the critical temperature Tc in the equilibrium. The olive line represents the second-order phase-transition line.

FIG. 2. Steady-state gap as a function of temperatures of the first bath T1 and second bath T2 for an s-wave supercon- ductor with strong inherent scattering γ1 ≈γ0, leading to a steady state well described by a temperature determined by the stationarity of energy, Eq. (12).

FIG. 3. Different steady state distribution of quasiparticles at the bath temperatures T1/Tc = 0.6 and T2/Tc = 1.2. Red curve (GGE) corresponds to the non-equilibrium steady state, stabilized by the interplay of the two baths, Eq (9). Dashed line (GE) represents the thermal occupation obtained from the energy rate equation (12) in case of strong inherent scat- tering γ1 ∼γ0. The blue and green curves correspond to thermal distributions at the temperatures of the two baths, reached if system would be coupled to only one of them.

FIG. 4. (a) Steady-state gap ∆∞/∆0 as a function two tem- perature baths T1 and T2 for d-wave superconductor. Dis- tribution of quasiparticles in the equilibrium at T1/Tc = T2/Tc = 0.1 (b), and in the steady state with T1/Tc = 1.7 and T2/Tc = 0.3 (c).

FIG. 5. Dependence of the steady state gap on the relative strength α = α+−/(α++ + α−−) of scattering and two-particle creation/annihilation term for the s-wave pairing case. Results for α = 1/4, 4 are comparable to the α = 1 considered in the main text, emphasising that our results are not fine tuned to a specific choice of α.
